topic.title: Microsoft Bought Nokia's Phones, Then Wrote Them Off

title: Nokia Was in Every Pocket. Microsoft Bought It Anyway
description:
Why did Microsoft buy Nokia's phone business, and why did it write the business down two years later?
Microsoft and Nokia, 2013 to 2015, told from the deal announcement and the write-off.
Sources: Microsoft, TechCrunch (Jul 2015).
Based on public records and reporting. Not financial or legal advice.

lines.text: Nokia was in every pocket. So why did Microsoft pay billions for it?
And Microsoft didn't buy it cheap. It paid €5.44B for the phones and the patents.
€3.79B bought the phone business itself. The other €1.65B paid to use Nokia's patents. So what were those phones really worth?
About 32,000 Nokia staff were set to move over with it, from a company born in Finland.
But Nokia's smartphones, the Lumias, ran Windows Phone. Not Android, and not the iPhone's system. So who would buy them?
Two summers later, Microsoft stopped trying to grow a phone business of its own. It cut 7,800 jobs, mostly in phones.
Then it wrote $7.6B off its books, on the phone business it had bought just two years before.
Nokia or iPhone: which was your first phone? The one in your hand runs Android or Apple's system. Before them, it was this.

All 6 facts confirmed on source pages: Microsoft 2013-09-03 release (EUR 5.44B total in cash, EUR 3.79B D&S, EUR 1.65B patent licence, ~32,000 staff expected to transfer); TechCrunch 2015-07-08 ($7.6B erased from books on the Nokia hardware purchase, 7,800 layoffs primarily in phones, Nadella: moving from a strategy to grow a standalone phone business). Verify list met: euros labelled, 'wrote off its books' for the impairment, no numeric market-share claim. New hook/title/thumbnail/labels checked: 'in every pocket' read as idiom for Nokia's era as top phone maker; 'pay billions for it' clarified next beat as phones + patents. Disclaimer ends description. Notes: title/hook 'it' could read as all of Nokia (Microsoft bought only the phone business; patents licensed); the hook's 'why' is not answered explicitly; plan cta and script cta differ slightly.

payoff: 'nearly the whole price of the deal' is an uncomputed comparison across currencies and is wrong by the sources: TechCrunch puts the deal at $7.2B (EUR 5.44B), so the $7.6B write-down is MORE than the whole price, and far more than the EUR 3.79B phone part. Drop the comparison or compute it in code from a sourced USD price (e.g. the 10-K's final purchase price).

payoff: '$7.6B ... gone in two years' presents an impairment as money lost; the topic's verify item says it was goodwill/asset impairment (TechCrunch: 'goodwill impairment'), not cash. Say it was written off the books, not 'gone'.

hook + title-adjacent line 'Microsoft bought it, and two years later, gone' and turn 'Microsoft gave up': in July 2015 the phone business was not gone; Nadella said Microsoft would 'run a more effective and focused phone portfolio' and was 'moving from a strategy to grow a standalone phone business' (TechCrunch). Lumias kept selling into 2016-17. Reword to what the source says (stopped trying to grow a standalone phone business; wrote it down).

Confirmed: EUR 5.44B total, EUR 3.79B Devices & Services, EUR 1.65B patent licence, ~32,000 staff (Microsoft press release page, opened); $7.6B write-down and 7,800 cuts primarily in phones (TechCrunch page, opened). Note: 'in every pocket' (hook, title) is an unsourced market-share hyperbole the topic's verify list warns about; soften or source it. Description ends with the disclaimer.
